newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian prime minister tells investors not to worry.
newsitem.headline: Indian prime minister tells investors not to worry.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Monday reassured foreign business leaders worried over the pace of economic reforms that his government was committed to welcoming foreign investment and spurring growth.

Deve Gowda repeatedly told a meeting of the Geneva-based World Economic Forum that his centre-left coalition would not reverse the free-market policies of the preceding government of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.

"The vision of this government is, first, to continue economic reforms," he said. "There is no question of a reversal of economic reforms....There should not be any confusion in the minds of foreign investors."
He reiterated his 13-party coalition's pledge to eventually attract $10 billion of foreign direct investment per year.
In 1994, India attracted $5.5 billion of net private capital inflows, largely portfolio investment in stocks not projects, compared to China's $46.6 billion, according to the World Bank.
Deve Gowda also restated his government's commitment to achieving 7.0 percent annual growth of gross domestic product (GDP) over the next decade.
"We are prepared to take all necessary steps with respect to political and other constraints to meet the (growth) target," Deve Gowda said. "That is our commitment."

Claude Smadja, managing director of the World Economic Forum, said Deve Gowda had showed he was a strong advocate of economic reform despite the divergent ideologies of his 13-party coalition, which ranges from free traders to communists.
"This is a strong message of the continuation of economic reforms," Smadja said. "I see a prime minister in a hurry to achieve economic growth."
Deve Gowda's renewed commitment to economic growth came amid mounting doubts about whether India will meet its target.
GDP growth in the 1995/96 fiscal year that ended on March 31 was recently revised downward to 6.3 percent from 7.0 percent, largely because of unexpectedly weak agricultural output.
Industrial production has been sluggish so far in 1996/97, especially in core industries such as power.

Many analysts consider the government's 1996/97 GDP growth target of 6.6 percent ambitious. They point to bottlenecks in key core sectors such as power and transport, and have questioned the government's commitment to ensuring high growth.
But Deve Gowda told executives attending a two-day meeting of the World Economic Forum not to worry. "We have made the promise of speedy growth, which is very essential," he said.
He said his government would soon draft a proposal to provide greater opportunity for private investment in agriculture, which he called critical to economic growth.

Deve Gowda said his government had streamlined procedures for approving foreign investment proposals by empowering the Industry Ministry to take decisions. Since his government took power in June, the ministry had cleared more than 500 projects involving foreign direct investment.
States had been given greater say over power projects to ensure there would be no delays or escalation of costs.

Asked by Smadja if India's legendary bureaucracy was an obtacle to reform, Deve Gowda offered a curt reply: "The bureaucracy is not a problem. The political will is not lacking. Please remove that kind of suspicion. That is my problem."
